Using dynastically to mean strictly or rigidly; it means by inherited succession within a ruling family.

senses.definition: Any of several large carnivorous and carrion-eating birds in the family Accipitridae, having a powerful hooked bill and keen vision.
senses.example: An eagle circled high above the canyon, scanning the valley floor for prey.

senses.definition: A score of two under par for a hole.
senses.example: I got an eagle in the third hole.

senses.definition: A gold coin with a face value of ten dollars, formerly used in the United States.
senses.example: The collector's cabinet held a gleaming gold eagle minted in 1907.

senses.definition: (historical) A 13th-century coin minted in Europe and circulated in England as a debased sterling silver penny, outlawed under Edward I of England.
senses.example: Medieval chroniclers complained that the debased eagle coins were circulating as sterling pennies across England.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To score an eagle.
senses.example: On the 14th hole, she eagled the par five with a perfect long iron.

core.definition: A large bird of prey with a strong hooked beak, broad wings and very keen eyesight.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and 'ea' is a long 'ee'. The second syllable is weak and sounds like 'gul', not 'gel'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: the eagle symbolizes strength, freedom, vision and national pride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eagle for the bird, most often the bald eagle, which is the national bird of the United States. Golfers also use eagle for a score of two under par on one hole. In everyday talk the bird is the first meaning people think of.

distinctions.note: Eagles are generally larger and more powerful, with heavier beaks and feet. Hawks are smaller, and Americans often say 'hawk' for a more slender bird of prey.
Vultures mostly feed on carrion and have bare heads. Eagles hunt live prey and are feathered on the head.

examples.everyday: We saw a bald eagle over the lake this morning, and the kids couldn't stop pointing at it.
examples.professional: The park service report confirmed a nesting pair of golden eagles in the north meadow this spring.
examples.analytical: The eagle has long served as a national symbol, its hooked beak and keen sight standing for vigilance and sovereignty.

nuance.analogy: An eagle is like a telescope with wings: it sees very far and very clearly from high above.
nuance.etymology: From Old French aigle, from Latin aquila, 'eagle'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'gel' instead of a weak 'gul'.
Mixing up eagle and hawk when describing birds in a yard or park.
Using eagle for golf scores without the context of par, which may confuse non-golfers.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word nesher (נֶשֶׁר) names the eagle in the Old Testament, and it can also refer to vultures in some passages. Eagles appear as images of God's care, renewal and protection. Exodus 19:4 describes God carrying Israel on eagles' wings, a picture of rescue and guidance. Deuteronomy 32:11 likens God to an eagle stirring up its nest and bearing its young on its wings. Isaiah 40:31 promises that those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles.

eagle.etymology: From Middle English *egle*, from Anglo-Norman *egle*, from Old French *aigle*, from Latin *aquila*.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the faith, practices, etc. of the Eastern Orthodox Church.

core.definition: Relating to the Eastern Orthodox Church, the family of self-governing churches that follow Byzantine tradition and are not under the pope.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on AWR in Orthodox, with a clear American r. Eastern has a lighter stress, and the -dox ending sounds like 'socks.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a formal religious label used in church, news and academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans capitalize Eastern Orthodox as a proper noun and use Orthodox alone in casual talk when the context is clear. Avoid calling every Orthodox Christian 'Greek Orthodox,' since many American Orthodox Christians have Russian, Serbian, Romanian, Antiochian or other backgrounds. Orthodox parishes in the US are often ethnic or multi-ethnic, so ask what a person's tradition is before assuming.

distinctions.note: Eastern Catholic churches use Eastern liturgies but are in communion with the pope, while Eastern Orthodox churches are not.
Lowercase orthodox means conforming to accepted belief or practice in general, whereas capitalized Eastern Orthodox names a specific church family.
Oriental Orthodox churches, such as the Armenian and Coptic churches, separated earlier over Christological questions and are not in communion with the Eastern Orthodox churches.

examples.everyday: My coworker's family is Eastern Orthodox, so they fast before Easter and go to church on a different schedule.
examples.professional: Our hospital chaplaincy team includes an Eastern Orthodox priest, so we plan staffing around their feast days.
examples.analytical: Eastern Orthodox theology has emphasized theosis, or union with God, as the center of salvation, and this shapes its sacramental life.

nuance.analogy: Like a family of sister churches that shares one ancient liturgy and one faith, with no single worldwide head but a shared sense of tradition.
nuance.etymology: Eastern from Old English ēastern; Orthodox from Greek orthodoxos, meaning right opinion or right praise.
common_mistakes: Calling the church 'Greek Orthodox' for every Orthodox Christian, which is inaccurate
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in or-THA-dox

senses.definition: A written work edited and published, as by a certain editor or in a certain manner, or at a certain time.
senses.example: She wanted a copy of the Clericotes edition, but had to settle for the 1921 edition. She had never liked abridged editions.

senses.definition: The whole number of copies of a work printed and published at one time.
senses.example: The first edition was soon sold.

senses.definition: An instance of the first or second sense.
senses.example: What he had found was a particularly valuable first edition.

senses.definition: A particular instance of an event.
senses.example: The 2014 edition of the Tour de France started in Leeds, Yorkshire.

core.definition: One version of a published work, such as a book or magazine, usually with changes or updates from earlier versions, or all copies printed at one time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, so the first syllable is a weak 'ih'. The ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a publishing fact and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use edition for a revised or updated version of a book, textbook, or software manual, such as 'the third edition'. For a single print run without changes, they often say printing or issue. For a newspaper released on a given day they say edition too, as in 'the morning edition'.

distinctions.note: A printing is one run of copies made at one time, and it may be unchanged; an edition is a version that has been revised or reset.
Version is broader and can refer to any form of a text or software; edition is specific to published works and usually implies a numbered or dated release.

examples.everyday: Did you get the new edition of that cookbook, or are you still using the old one?
examples.professional: Please send the revised edition of the policy manual to the whole team before Friday.
examples.analytical: Each new edition of a textbook reveals how the discipline itself has changed its assumptions and priorities.

nuance.analogy: An edition is like a new model year of a car: the same design line, but with updates and corrections built in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin editio, 'a giving out, publication', from edere, 'to give out'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the edition of the book' when you mean the copy you own; you can say 'my edition' or 'this edition'.
Confusing edition with edit; an edition is a published version, while to edit is the act of changing a text.

edition.etymology: From French *édition*, from Latin *ēditiō*, from *ēdere* (“to publish”).

senses.definition: Requiring or showing effort.

core.definition: Requiring or showing a lot of effort; taking real work and attention to accomplish.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on EF. The 'r' is clear, and the final '-ful' is a reduced 'fuhl', not 'fool'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes the amount of work without praising or criticizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'effortful' in psychology, education and academic writing, for example 'effortful processing'. In everyday speech they say 'hard', 'tiring' or 'laborious'. The word is not wrong in conversation, but it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Laborious implies slow, tedious work and often a negative sense of drudgery, while effortful is neutral about the work's quality.
Strenuous describes physically demanding activity, while effortful can refer to mental or physical work.
Difficult describes how hard something is in general, while effortful stresses the effort it takes to do it.

examples.everyday: Pushing that old couch up the stairs was pretty effortful, so we took a break halfway.
examples.professional: Writing the documentation is effortful, but it saves hours of confusion for the next engineer.
examples.analytical: Psychologists distinguish automatic processing from effortful processing, which requires conscious attention and draws on limited working memory.

nuance.analogy: Like carrying a heavy backpack up a steep trail, compared with walking on a flat road.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the noun 'effort' with the suffix '-ful', meaning full of or marked by.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'effortful' with 'effortless', which means needing no effort.
Using 'effortful' for every hard task in casual speech, where 'hard' or 'tiring' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The shell around an egg.
senses.example: She cracked the eggshell against the bowl and let the yolk slide in.

senses.definition: A pale off-white color, like that of the eggshell of many chickens.
senses.example: eggshell:

senses.definition: Of a pale yellowish-whitish color, like that of the eggshell.
senses.example: We painted the nursery walls an eggshell white that softened the afternoon light.

senses.definition: Exhibiting the thinness, translucency or near-transparency, and fragility of an eggshell.
senses.example: eggshell porcelain

senses.definition: Very matt, having a low reflexivity, like an eggshell.
senses.example: This clear varnish is available in gloss, matt and eggshell finishes.

core.definition: The hard, thin outer covering of an egg; also a pale off-white color, or a soft matte paint finish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'EHG'. The 'sh' is a single clear sound, and the final 'l' is a light syllable, not a full 'ul' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive, everyday word, and the figurative uses are mostly positive or cautionary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'eggshell' most often as the shell of an egg, and in home improvement stores it names a satin-like, slightly sheen paint finish, which is common in houses. The color sense describes a soft off-white, like the color of many brown or white eggs. The idiom 'walk on eggshells' means to be very careful not to upset someone.

distinctions.note: Shell is the general word for a hard outer covering on many animals and objects; eggshell refers specifically to eggs.
Ivory is a warm, creamy white; eggshell is a paler, slightly yellowish or grayish off-white.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that bowl, there are bits of eggshell floating in it.
examples.professional: Can we use an eggshell finish on the conference room walls, since it hides fingerprints better than gloss?
examples.analytical: The peace talks rested on an eggshell of goodwill, fragile enough to break at the first provocation.

nuance.analogy: Like a thin protective case that looks solid but cracks under sudden pressure.
nuance.etymology: Compound of egg and shell, from Old English ǣg and scell.
common_mistakes: Writing 'egg shell' as two words in a noun phrase where the compound is written as one word.
Saying 'walk on egg shells' instead of 'walk on eggshells' in the idiom.

eggshell.etymology: From Middle English *eggeshell*, *ege schelle*, *egg-shel*, *egg shelle* (also as, *ey-schel*, *ey-schelle*), partially continuing Old English *ǣġsċill*, *ǣġsċyll* (“eggshell”), equivalent to *egg* + *shell*.

senses.definition: Acronym of Executable and Linking Format, a common object file format for Unix.
Initialism of extremely low frequency.
senses.example: The navy uses ELF signals to reach submarines deep below the ocean surface.

senses.definition: Acronym of English as a lingua franca (“English used by non-native speakers”).
senses.example: Our global team communicates in ELF, so nobody feels disadvantaged by accent.

core.definition: Executable and Linking Format, the standard file format for compiled programs, shared libraries and object code on Linux and other Unix-like systems.

pronunciation.tip: Americans spell out the letters E-L-F, with the main stress on the final F, instead of saying the word 'elf'. Keep each letter name short and clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Programmers, system administrators and data engineers use ELF constantly, as in 'the binary is an ELF file' or 'check the ELF header'. The lowercase word 'elf' means the fantasy creature, and in other fields ELF can mean 'extremely low frequency' (radio communication) or 'English as a lingua franca', so context matters. In a meeting, say 'ELF binary' or 'ELF file' to be clear.

distinctions.note: PE is the executable format used by Windows, while ELF is the format used by Linux and most other Unix-like systems.
Mach-O is the executable format used by macOS and iOS, so an ELF file will not run natively on a Mac.

examples.everyday: My Mac can't run that file because it's an ELF binary built for Linux.
examples.professional: Can you confirm the build artifact is ELF before we push it to the Linux staging servers?
examples.analytical: The ELF specification defines a file header, program headers and section headers that the loader uses to map a binary into memory.

nuance.analogy: An ELF file is like a shipping box with a label that tells the loader where each part belongs.
nuance.etymology: The letters stand for Executable and Linking Format, a Unix System V format; it is an acronym, not a word.
common_mistakes: Saying the word 'elf' when the file format is spelled out as E-L-F.
Confusing the technical ELF with the fantasy creature when talking about software.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or producing elimination.
senses.example: The eliminative power of the storm.

core.definition: Tending to remove or get rid of something, or involving the process of eliminating unwanted elements or possibilities.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIM, the second syllable. The -ative ending is pronounced 'uh-tiv', with the a reduced to schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process or method and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: You will see eliminative mostly in medicine, such as an eliminative diet, in research methods, and in philosophy, as in eliminative reasoning. Everyday Americans usually say elimination or removal instead, so the adjective sounds technical and precise.

distinctions.note: Elimination is the noun for the act or result of removing something, while eliminative is the adjective that describes a process or method.
Exclusive means only one option can be included, while eliminative describes removing what is unwanted or false.

examples.everyday: My doctor suggested an eliminative diet to find out which food is making me sick.
examples.professional: We used an eliminative approach, removing one feature at a time until the error disappeared.
examples.analytical: Eliminative reasoning proceeds by ruling out rival hypotheses rather than confirming one favored explanation directly.

nuance.analogy: An eliminative process works like a sieve, letting the unwanted particles fall through until only what you need remains.
nuance.etymology: From eliminate plus -ive, from Latin eliminare, 'to drive out'.
common_mistakes: Using eliminative as a noun; the noun is elimination.
Using eliminative in casual speech, where elimination or removal sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Lacking emotion.

core.definition: Showing or feeling no emotion; cold, detached, or unmoved by what is happening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MOH, not on the first. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', and the final -less is a reduced 'lus'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It often suggests coldness or an unwillingness to show feeling, so it can sound critical when describing a person. In a neutral context, such as a report of how someone looked, it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use emotionless to describe a face, voice, or manner that shows no feeling, often in a news story or in a conversation about a movie character or a coworker who seems hard to read. It is more everyday than 'impassive' and less clinical than 'detached'. It can sound harsh if said about a real person in front of them, so Americans often soften it with 'a little' or 'kind of'.

distinctions.note: Stoic describes someone who endures pain or hardship calmly and deliberately, while emotionless describes a lack of feeling that may not be a choice.
Detached describes someone who is not personally involved in a situation, while emotionless focuses on the absence of visible feeling.
Impassive is a more formal word for showing no visible reaction, and it is more common in writing than in speech.

examples.everyday: My brother got the bad news about his job, and he just stayed emotionless the whole time.
examples.professional: In the meeting, the director's emotionless tone made it hard for the team to tell whether she was upset about the delay.
examples.analytical: The narrator's emotionless prose forces the reader to supply the grief that the character refuses to show.

nuance.analogy: Like a poker player's face: nothing shows on the surface, even when something is happening underneath.
nuance.etymology: From emotion plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without', from Old English leas.
common_mistakes: Confusing emotionless (no feeling) with emotional (full of feeling, or easily upset).
Stressing the first syllable as EE-mo-shun-less; the stress belongs on MOH.

senses.definition: Giving courage, confidence or hope; auspicious.
senses.example: Although there is no cure for the disease yet, the research results are encouraging.

senses.definition: Supporting by giving encouragement: positively.
senses.example: Your encouraging words inspired me to persevere.

senses.definition: Encouragement.
senses.example: Her steady encouraging during those hard months kept me going through school.

core.definition: Giving hope, confidence or support, or showing that things are going well.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KUR, the second syllable. The middle vowel is reduced to 'ij' and the final -ing is a short /ɪŋ/, not 'ang'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes results, words or signs that boost morale.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say that's encouraging to respond to good news, progress reports or hopeful signs, often in a calm, understated tone. It is common in meetings, medical updates and casual conversation. Overusing it can sound like a polite brush-off if the news is actually mixed.

distinctions.note: Promising suggests future success, while encouraging suggests the current situation gives reason for hope and confidence.
Uplifting is mainly emotional and often describes music, stories or speeches, while encouraging often describes facts, results or support.
Encouraged describes how a person feels, while encouraging describes the thing that causes the feeling.

examples.everyday: The first test results are encouraging, so I'm not too worried about the next one.
examples.professional: The pilot numbers are encouraging, so we should expand to two more regions next quarter.
examples.analytical: Encouraging early results can tempt researchers to overinterpret a small sample, so they must test the hypothesis again.

nuance.analogy: An encouraging result is like a green light at the first intersection: it does not guarantee the whole trip, but it tells you to keep going.
nuance.etymology: From encourage, from Old French encoragier, from corage, courage.
common_mistakes: Confusing encouraging with encouraged; say I'm encouraged for a feeling and it's encouraging for the thing that causes it.
Pronouncing the ending as ang instead of the short ing sound.

senses.definition: To amuse (someone); to engage the attention of agreeably.
senses.example: to entertain friends with lively conversation

senses.definition: To have someone over at one's home, or some other venue, for a party or visit.
senses.example: They enjoy entertaining a lot.

senses.definition: To receive and take into consideration; to have a thought in mind.
senses.example: The committee would like to entertain the idea of reducing the budget figures.

core.definition: To amuse or hold someone's attention in a pleasant way, or to host guests at your home or another venue.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, TAIN. The middle -ter is a light, reduced American r-colored vowel, and the t is a flap in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests kindness and pleasant hospitality, though to entertain an idea or offer means to consider it seriously, which is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say we like to entertain when they mean hosting dinner parties or having friends over, and they often use it to describe a host's skill. When used of children or guests, it means keeping them amused. In a formal setting, an offer might be entertained, meaning considered seriously, but in everyday talk people say think about it.

distinctions.note: Amuse focuses on making someone laugh or smile, while entertain can also mean hosting people or holding their attention for longer.
Host focuses on being the person who welcomes guests and organizes an event, while entertain focuses on what happens during the visit.
Consider means to think carefully about something, and it is more neutral than entertain, which in formal use suggests you are open to an idea.

examples.everyday: We love to entertain on weekends, so our backyard is usually full of friends and their kids.
examples.professional: Our sales team will entertain clients at the conference dinner, so please keep Thursday evening free.
examples.analytical: Descartes asks whether we should entertain the possibility that our senses deceive us, and he argues that we must examine it carefully.

nuance.analogy: To entertain is like keeping a pot of coffee warm on the stove, always ready and welcoming for whoever comes through the door.
nuance.etymology: From French entretenir, from entre- (among, between) and tenir (to hold), meaning to hold among or keep up.
common_mistakes: Using entertain with a direct object meaning to have fun, as in I entertained very much at the party, when the correct form is I enjoyed myself.
Saying entertain me in the sense of please entertain my question, which sounds strange; use consider instead.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Greek philoxenia (love of strangers) is the root of hospitality, and the idea of entertaining guests appears when people welcome visitors who turn out to be messengers from God. Hebrews 13:2 urges believers to show hospitality to strangers, reminding them that some people have unknowingly welcomed angels. Genesis 18:1-8 describes Abraham hosting three visitors by the oaks of Mamre with generous food and care. Romans 12:13 calls Christians to practice hospitality as part of sharing with fellow believers in need.

entertain.etymology: From Middle English *entertenen*, from Middle French *entretenir*, from Old French *entretenir*, from *entre* (“among”) + *tenir* (“to hold”), from Latin *inter* + *teneō* (“hold, keep”).

senses.definition: The act of enthralling or the state of being enthralled.

core.definition: The state of being completely captivated, or the power that holds someone spellbound.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on THRAWL, and the first syllable is a short 'in', not 'en' as in the verb spelling. The final -ment is reduced to 'mənt', and the th is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests delight or wonder, though it can imply a loss of freedom when someone is held in its power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use enthrallment in conversation; it is mostly found in literary criticism, essays and formal writing. In everyday speech, people say fascination, captivation or 'being hooked'. Use it when you want a more elevated or vivid noun than 'fascination'.

distinctions.note: Fascination is more common and can be mild, while enthrallment is stronger and implies being completely held.
Captivation suggests attraction through charm, while enthrallment suggests an overwhelming, almost spellbinding control.
Obsession is usually negative and suggests a compulsive fixation, while enthrallment can be pleasant and temporary.

examples.everyday: Watching the fireworks over the lake filled the kids with pure enthrallment.
examples.professional: Her demo produced a kind of enthrallment in the room, but I was wary of the hype.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of the soul's enthrallment to created things treats desire as a kind of captivity that only God can free.

nuance.analogy: Like a spell cast over a room: everyone is held, and no one wants the spell to break.
nuance.etymology: From enthrall plus -ment; enthrall comes from en- and thrall, from Old Norse þræll, 'slave, servant'.
common_mistakes: Using enthrallment to describe a person who is captivated; the adjective enthralled is the natural form.
Stressing the first syllable as IN-thrall-ment instead of in-THRAWL-ment.

senses.definition: Causing a trance-like state; hypnotic.
senses.example: The hypnotist's slow, rhythmic counting was entrancing, and soon the volunteer's eyelids began to flutter shut.

senses.definition: Causing ecstasy or rapture; enrapturing; charming.
senses.example: Her performance of the old folk ballad was entrancing, and the whole audience sat motionless.

senses.definition: The process by which somebody is entranced.
senses.example: The entrancing of the audience happened so gradually that no one noticed the magician's technique.

core.definition: Extremely charming or attractive, so that you find it hard to stop watching or listening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRAN, the second syllable. The final -ing is a short 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something beautiful, charming or captivating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entrancing for a voice, a view, a smile or a story that holds attention. It is more vivid and less common than enchanting in everyday speech. It can sound a little dramatic in casual business settings, so use it when the praise is sincere.

distinctions.note: Enchanting is more common and softer in everyday speech. Entrancing suggests deeper absorption and a stronger hold on attention.
Hypnotic describes something repetitive that holds attention and can be neutral or negative. Entrancing is almost always positive.
Captivating is close in meaning and is common in reviews and marketing. Entrancing sounds more poetic.

examples.everyday: Her laugh is absolutely entrancing, and I could listen to her all night.
examples.professional: The keynote opened with an entrancing demo that held the room for twenty minutes.
examples.analytical: Gadamer finds in art an entrancing power that shows us a truth beyond method.

nuance.analogy: An entrancing melody is like a song you cannot stop humming, one that pulls you back in again and again.
nuance.etymology: From the verb entrance plus the -ing ending.
common_mistakes: Confusing entrancing with entering, which is a different word.
Using entrancing for something merely interesting, when the word implies strong fascination.

senses.definition: A person who, or thing that eradicates.

core.definition: A person or thing that completely destroys or removes something harmful, such as a disease, pest or problem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAD, and reduce the unstressed vowels. The -ate ending is a clear 'ayt', and the final -or is an unstressed rhotic /ɚ/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually describes someone or something that wipes out a serious problem, though it can be negative when describing someone who destroys things of value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing, reports, speeches and history. In everyday speech they would say 'exterminator' for a pest-control worker or 'something that gets rid of' a problem. The word can be used sarcastically or in a critical sense for a leader who destroys institutions.

distinctions.note: An exterminator is a pest-control worker who kills vermin, while an eradicator can be a person, program or force that removes any serious problem.
An eliminator removes something from consideration or a competition, while an eradicator destroys something completely at its root.

examples.everyday: Our pest guy is a real eradicator; the mice are gone and they haven't come back.
examples.professional: The new vaccine program has become an eradicator of measles in our region, which the health department now tracks.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the reformer was a true eradicator of corruption or merely its redistributor under a new name.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire crew that puts out a fire completely, leaving no embers to start it again.
nuance.etymology: From eradicate, from Latin eradicare, 'to pull out by the root', from ex- 'out' and radix 'root'.
common_mistakes: Using eradicator for an ordinary cleaning product; in American English that sense usually uses 'remover' or 'cleaner'.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: A hermit; a religious recluse, someone who lives alone.

core.definition: A person who lives alone, apart from society, usually for religious reasons; a hermit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say it quickly as 'uh'. Americans rhyme the last syllable with 'light', not 'mite' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a choice of solitude and can suggest holiness or eccentricity depending on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. You will meet it in religious history, literature, or writing about monks and mystics. In everyday speech, say 'hermit' or 'someone who lives alone in the woods'. Using 'eremite' in casual talk may sound bookish.

distinctions.note: 'Hermit' is the common everyday word for the same thing. 'Eremite' is more formal and mostly appears in religious or scholarly writing.
A recluse avoids people for personal or psychological reasons and need not be religious, while an eremite withdraws for spiritual purposes.

examples.everyday: My neighbor acts like an eremite since his wife passed, but he waves at me every morning.
examples.professional: In the seminary history seminar, our professor described the early eremite communities in the Egyptian desert.
examples.analytical: The early Christian eremite rejected the city not out of hatred for society but in pursuit of undivided attention to God.

nuance.analogy: An eremite is a hermit with a monastery's worth of history behind the word.
nuance.etymology: From Greek erēmitēs, 'of the desert', from erēmos, 'desert, solitary'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ear' with a long vowel; it is closer to 'air'.
Using 'eremite' in casual speech where 'hermit' sounds more natural.

eremite.etymology: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin *eremita*, from Ancient Greek *ἐρημίτης*, from *ἐρῆμος* + *ίτης*.

senses.definition: To eject something violently (such as lava or water, as from a volcano or geyser).
senses.example: The volcano erupted, spewing lava across a wide area.

senses.definition: To burst forth; to break out.
senses.example: The third molar tooth erupts late in most people, and sometimes does not appear at all.

senses.definition: To spontaneously release pressure or tension.
senses.example: The crowd erupted in anger.

senses.definition: (Of birds, insects, etc.) To suddenly appear in a certain region in large numbers.
senses.example: Thousands of blackbirds erupted over the cornfield at dusk, darkening the sky.

core.definition: To burst out suddenly and violently, like a volcano, or to break out into strong emotion or action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, RUPT. The final pt is one cluster with no extra vowel, and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative or intense. It often describes sudden anger, violence, or loud reactions, though it can also describe a happy outburst such as applause.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use erupt for volcanoes and for sudden emotions or events, such as The crowd erupted in cheers. In casual talk you might say that someone blew up or lost it when angry, but erupt is a common word in news and conversation. The word is intransitive in most everyday uses, so you say the volcano erupted rather than erupted the lava.

distinctions.note: Explode suggests a fast, forceful blast, often of something stored, while erupt suggests pressure breaking out, often from below or within.
Burst is a more general word for breaking open suddenly, while erupt is often used for volcanoes, violence, or strong emotion.

examples.everyday: The whole room erupted into laughter when the dog walked onto the stage.
examples.professional: The meeting erupted into argument when the budget numbers finally appeared on the screen.
examples.analytical: Political tensions erupt when long-suppressed grievances find a public occasion, which is why the spark seems sudden but the pressure was building for years.

nuance.analogy: Erupt is like a shaken soda bottle that finally blows its cap when the pressure can no longer stay inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin erumpere, to break out, from e-, out, and rumpere, to break.
common_mistakes: Confusing erupt with interrupt; they look alike but mean very different things.
Using erupt with a direct object, as in the crowd erupted the cheers; say the crowd erupted into cheers.
Saying ih-RUP-ted with an extra syllable in the past tense; the past tense is erupted, pronounced ih-RUP-tid.

erupt.etymology: From Latin *eruptus*, past participle of *ērumpō* (“to break out, to burst out”), from *e* (“out”) + *rumpō* (“to break”).

core.definition: The Greek and Latin form of Ezra, used in the titles of 1 and 2 Esdras, books outside the Hebrew Bible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: EZ-druhs. The 's' after 'z' is a clear 'd' sound, and the last syllable is a reduced 'duhs', not 'dras' as in 'drab'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Mostly encountered in discussions of the Apocrypha and Septuagint. Numbering is confusing, so scholars specify which edition they mean. Americans typically say 'Ezra' for the canonical book.

distinctions.note: Ezra is the Hebrew form used for the canonical book; Esdras is the Greek and Latin form used for related books.
Nehemiah is a separate figure and book, though in some old numbering it was called 2 Esdras.
Apocrypha is the broader group of books; 1 and 2 Esdras are two of them in the RSV Apocrypha.

examples.everyday: My Bible includes the Apocrypha, so I noticed there's a book called 2 Esdras.
examples.professional: In today's seminar, we'll compare the numbering of Esdras in the Greek, Latin and English traditions.
examples.analytical: 2 Esdras blends Jewish apocalyptic reflection on suffering and theodicy with later Christian additions.

nuance.analogy: Like a name spelled differently in another language: Ezra in Hebrew, Esdras in Greek.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Esdras, a form of the Hebrew name Ezra ('help').
common_mistakes: Saying 'ES-dras' with a short 'a' like 'drab'.
Assuming Esdras is the same as the canonical book of Ezra.
Mixing up the numbering across different Bibles.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV Apocrypha includes 1 Esdras (a Greek retelling of the Judean return from exile) and 2 Esdras (an apocalyptic work with visions). The Hebrew Ezra, 'Yahweh helps,' is the scribe in the canonical book of Ezra, who read the law to the people (Ezra 7:6, 10; Nehemiah 8:1-3).

traditions.view: Orthodox Bibles generally include 1 Esdras as part of the canon, while 2 Esdras is usually in an appendix and not treated as fully canonical.
Catholics do not consider 1 or 2 Esdras (Latin 3 and 4 Esdras) canonical; they appear in the Vulgate appendix, and the canonical books are Ezra and Nehemiah.
Protestants do not treat the Esdras books as Scripture. Anglicans may read them as Apocrypha for instruction, but not to establish doctrine; the RSV Apocrypha includes them.

senses.definition: Fair and impartial; unbiased; just.
senses.example: The questioners are not evenhanded in dealing with the candidates.

core.definition: Treating all sides or people fairly and equally, without favoring one over another.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on EE in 'even,' with secondary stress on HAN in 'handed.' Do not say 'ee-ven' with a long second syllable; the middle syllable is a reduced 'uhn.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises fairness and impartiality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evenhanded to describe judges, referees, journalists, managers, and anyone expected to be neutral. It often appears in phrases like 'an evenhanded approach' or 'evenhanded treatment.' In everyday talk people also say 'fair' or 'fair-minded,' which is more casual.

distinctions.note: Fair is more general and everyday, while evenhanded stresses equal treatment of parties in a dispute.
Impartial is more formal and emphasizes having no stake in the outcome; evenhanded emphasizes how one behaves toward each side.

examples.everyday: My dad is evenhanded when my brother and I argue, so we both trust him to be fair.
examples.professional: The team lead needs an evenhanded approach when deciding which project gets the new budget.
examples.analytical: A genuinely evenhanded account must represent each position in its strongest form before evaluating it.

nuance.analogy: Like a scale that stays level when both sides are weighed equally, an evenhanded person gives each side the same treatment.
nuance.etymology: From even (level, equal) and handed, a compound formed in English.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, even handed, in formal writing; the standard spelling is evenhanded.
Stressing the second syllable of even as a long ee sound.

senses.definition: A religious service, most commonly seen in the Anglican or Episcopal Church, that takes place in the early hours of the evening; originally, and sometimes still, an alternative name for vespers or a service combining vespers and compline.
senses.example: The choir sang psalms at evensong, and the candles glowed softly in the old chapel.

core.definition: An evening worship service in the Anglican or Episcopal tradition, built around psalms, readings and canticles.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, with a lighter stress on 'song'. The middle syllable is a reduced 'in' sound, and many Americans pronounce the final vowel as 'aw' or 'ah' depending on accent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It carries a religious and traditional tone and is most likely to appear in church settings or in discussions of liturgy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'evensong' mainly in Episcopal and Anglican churches or when talking about church music and liturgy. Most people outside those churches would say 'evening prayer' or 'vespers' instead. You may hear it in a casual conversation about a choir concert, but it is rare outside church contexts.

distinctions.note: Vespers is the older and broader term used in Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, while evensong is the Anglican name for its evening office.
Evening prayer is the more common Episcopal name in modern prayer books, while evensong is more traditional and often sung.

examples.everyday: We went to choral evensong at the cathedral last Sunday, and the singing was beautiful.
examples.professional: The music director scheduled the choir for evensong on the first Sunday of Advent.
examples.analytical: Evensong in the Book of Common Prayer preserves the evening office, drawing on psalms and canticles that echo ancient monastic practice.

nuance.analogy: Evensong is like a sunset hymn that closes the church day, the way a lullaby closes the home day.
nuance.etymology: From Old English æfensang, 'evening song'.
common_mistakes: Using 'evensong' for any evening church service; it refers specifically to Anglican or Episcopal worship.
Spelling it as 'evensongs' in the singular sense; 'evensong' is usually uncountable or used with 'an evensong' for a particular service.
nuance.biblical_note: Evensong draws on the Hebrew minḥah, 'offering' or 'gift', which named the evening sacrifice in Israel's worship. Psalm 141:2 speaks of the lifting up of hands as the evening sacrifice. Its canticles include the Magnificat, Luke 1:46-55, and the Nunc Dimittis, Luke 2:29-32.

traditions.view: The evening office is called Vespers, and it is one of the daily services in the cycle of prayer. It usually includes psalms, litanies and the lighting of lamps.

The evening prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours is called Vespers, and it includes psalms, a reading, a canticle and intercessions. Its use is central to the daily prayer of clergy and religious communities.

Anglican and Episcopal churches use Evensong or Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer. Lutheran and Reformed churches have their own vespers or evening prayer forms, and many free churches do not have a set evening liturgy.

senses.definition: In an exacting manner.

core.definition: In a way that demands great precision, care, or high standards from oneself or others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, ZAK. Don't add a separate sound for the t; it blends into the ng, so say it as one smooth run of sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes demanding standards, which can read as admirable or as harsh depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing, reviews, and formal description, not in casual speech. In conversation they usually say 'really strict' or 'very demanding' instead. You might hear it in a review of a restaurant, a film, or a manager's style.

distinctions.note: Strictly describes following rules or limits closely; exactingly describes demanding high standards of quality or performance.
Precisely focuses on accuracy of detail; exactingly focuses on how demanding the standards are.

examples.everyday: My sister's wedding planner was exactingly picky about the flower arrangements.
examples.professional: Our QA lead reviews every release exactingly before it goes to production.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues exactingly for a distinction between divine and human agency.

nuance.analogy: Like a jeweler who checks each stone under a loupe, working exactingly means refusing to accept anything less than fine work.
nuance.etymology: From exacting (demanding, from exact) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using exactingly for everyday speech, where 'strictly' or 'very carefully' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with exactly, which means precisely or agreed.

senses.definition: Something that is representative of all such things in a group.
Something that serves to illustrate or explain a rule.
senses.example: The textbook gave a clear example of how to apply the rule.

senses.definition: Something that serves as a pattern of behavior to be imitated (a good example) or not to be imitated (a bad example).
senses.example: Nelson Mandela was an example for many to follow.

senses.definition: A person punished as a warning to others.
senses.example: The judge sentenced him harshly to serve as an example for others.

senses.definition: A parallel or closely similar case, especially when serving as a precedent or model.
senses.example: This ruling sets an example for future courts facing similar disputes.

senses.definition: An instance (as a problem to be solved) serving to illustrate the rule or precept or to act as an exercise in the application of the rule.
senses.example: Work through the first example before attempting the homework problems.

senses.definition: To be illustrated or exemplified (by). (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The city's rebuilding efforts are exampled by its new waterfront parks.

core.definition: A thing or person that shows what a whole group, rule or idea is like, or a model to copy or avoid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the stem, ZAM. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so the word ends with a soft 'pul', not a full 'pal'. Start with ig, not eks.

nuance.connotation: Neutral by default; a 'good example' is positive and a 'bad example' is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use example constantly in conversation and teaching: 'Can you give me an example?' or 'for example.' 'Set an example' and 'a good example' are common phrases for behavior that others should follow. 'For instance' is a close alternative in spoken English. The verb sense, to be illustrated, is rare in everyday use.

distinctions.note: An instance is a single occurrence of something; an example is chosen to illustrate a general point or serve as a model.
A sample is a small part taken to represent a whole, especially in data or products; an example illustrates a rule, behavior or idea.

examples.everyday: Can you give me an example? I don't really understand what you mean by 'a good deal'.
examples.professional: Let me give you an example from last quarter's churn data to show why the metric misled us.
examples.analytical: Kant's example of the lying promise illustrates how a maxim fails when we try to universalize it.

nuance.analogy: Like a map that shows the general terrain with one clear landmark pointed out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exemplum, 'sample, model', from eximere, 'to take out'.
common_mistakes: Using 'example' where 'instance' fits better, as in 'an example of the event happened yesterday'.
Writing 'for example' with a comma incorrectly; in American English it usually follows a comma or starts a sentence, as in 'For example, the store opens late.'

example.etymology: From Middle English *example*, *exaumple*, from Old French *example*, *essaumple*, from Latin *exemplum* (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”); see *exempt*.

senses.definition: Synonym of excellence; the quality of being excellent.
senses.example: The judges praised the excellency of her research on protein folding.

core.definition: A formal title of honor for certain high officials, such as ambassadors or governors; also an older word for excellence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, 'EK.' The final syllable is a reduced 'see,' and the middle vowels are weak, so keep them quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful when used as a title; otherwise dated and somewhat formal.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, Excellency is used as a form of address for ambassadors, governors, and some foreign officials, as in 'Your Excellency.' As a general word for excellence, it is archaic and mainly appears in older texts or the Bible. Modern speakers would normally say excellence.

distinctions.note: Excellence is the everyday word for quality; excellency is mainly a title or an archaic form of the same idea.
Honorable is a title for many officials in the US, while Excellency is used for ambassadors and governors in formal address.

examples.everyday: When the ambassador visited our town, we all called him Your Excellency.
examples.professional: The letter was addressed to His Excellency, the consul general.
examples.analytical: Older translations render the Greek term as excellency, though the modern word excellence captures its meaning more clearly.

nuance.analogy: Like a formal name badge that signals rank rather than everyday quality.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excellentia, the same root as excellence, with the title sense developing in the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Using 'excellency' for everyday praise, where 'excellence' is correct.
Using 'Excellency' as a title without the proper 'His' or 'Your' before it.
nuance.biblical_note: The word excellency appears in older English Bibles, such as the King James translation, for Hebrew terms meaning majesty or splendor. The modern RSV generally uses words such as majesty or glory in these places, so the term is best understood as an archaic rendering.

senses.definition: The act or process of exhaling; breathing out.
senses.example: short exhalations of breath

senses.definition: That which is exhaled, or which rises in the form of vapor, fume, or steam.
senses.example: exhalations from the earth or flowers

senses.definition: A bright phenomenon; a meteor.
senses.example: The bright exhalation streaked across the night sky, startling the farmers in the valley.

core.definition: The act of breathing out air from the lungs, or the air that is breathed out.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the 'lay' syllable, and the first syllable has secondary stress. The 'h' is pronounced after the 'x' sound, and the ending is 'shun,' not 'shawn' or 'SHAY-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical action without emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'exhalation' mostly in medical, yoga, singing, or science contexts. In casual talk people usually say 'breathing out' or 'exhale' instead. The word can sound stiff or clinical in everyday conversation, but it is perfectly correct in writing and formal speech.

distinctions.note: 'Exhale' is the verb for the action, while 'exhalation' is the noun for the act or the breath itself.
'Breath' is the general word for air moving in and out of the lungs and is far more common in everyday speech.
'Inhalation' is the opposite action, breathing in air or vapor into the lungs.

examples.everyday: She let out a long exhalation after the bad news, and then she smiled a little.
examples.professional: The respiratory therapist asked the patient to count each exhalation during the breathing exercise.
examples.analytical: In her essay on prayer, she treats each exhalation as a sign of the self yielding what it has received.

nuance.analogy: Like a bellows pushing out the air it has just drawn in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exhalare, 'to breathe out', from ex- 'out' and halare 'to breathe'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'ek-suh-LAY-shun' with a weak 'lay', or 'EX-uh-lay-shun'.
Using 'exhalation' in casual talk where 'breathing out' sounds more natural.
Dropping the 'h' or saying 'ek-sha-LAY-shun' with a 'sh' sound.

exhalation.etymology: From Latin *exhālātiō*, from *exhālō* (“to breathe out, to exhale”), from *hālō* (“to breathe”).

senses.definition: A collection of propositions that, taken together, explain another proposition (the explanandum).

core.definition: In philosophy of science and logic, the set of statements that together explain or account for another statement, the explanandum.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'PLAY,' and the ending is pronounced 'nanz,' with the '-ans' ending sounding like 'anz.' Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized philosophical term, used mainly in discussions of scientific explanation and deductive-nomological models. Americans in casual conversation would not use it, and in academic writing it is almost always paired with 'explanandum.' Its plural is usually 'explanans' or 'explanantia.'

distinctions.note: An explanation is the act or result of explaining; an explanans is specifically the set of premises that do the explaining in a logical model.
The explanans does the explaining; the explanandum is what is explained.

collocations: the explanans must entail the explanandum

examples.everyday: My philosophy friend said the rules were the explanans, and the outcome of the game was what they were supposed to explain.
examples.professional: In our model review, the explanans consisted of three assumptions about user behavior that together predicted the spike.
examples.analytical: A deductive-nomological explanation succeeds only when the explanans includes at least one law of nature and the explanandum follows logically from it.

nuance.analogy: The explanans is like the set of reasons a judge lists that together justify a verdict.
nuance.etymology: From Latin explanans, the present participle of explanare, 'explaining.'
common_mistakes: Using explanans to mean the thing that is explained, which is the explanandum
Treating it as a synonym for explanation in everyday talk

senses.definition: The act of expelling or the state of being expelled.
senses.example: The scandal involved every member of the high school's football team, resulting in a flurry of expulsions, starting with the quarterback.

core.definition: The act of forcing someone to leave a place, group, or school, often as an official punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPUL, the second syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'shun', not 'shen' or 'shin'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes a serious, forced removal, often as a penalty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expulsion for students kicked out of school, members removed from a club, or people forced out of a country. In schools, 'suspension' is a milder, temporary punishment, while expulsion is permanent. In casual talk, people often say 'kicked out' instead.

distinctions.note: Suspension is temporary removal; expulsion is usually permanent or long-term removal.
Deportation is the removal of a person from a country by legal authority; expulsion is a broader term for forced removal from any place or group.

examples.everyday: My son got into trouble at school, and we were scared it might end in expulsion.
examples.professional: HR will review the policy before any expulsion from the employee resource group is decided.
examples.analytical: The theologian argued that the expulsion from Eden marks the loss of immediate access to God, not the loss of God's care.

nuance.analogy: Expulsion is like being shown the door: you are not just asked to leave, you are removed for good.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expulsio, from expellere, 'to drive out', from ex- 'out' plus pellere 'to drive'.
common_mistakes: Using expulsion as a verb; the verb is expel.
Confusing expulsion with suspension, which is temporary.

expulsion.etymology: From Middle English *expulsioun*, from Old French *expulsion*, from Latin *expulsiō*.

senses.definition: Exceeding the bounds of something; roving; hence, foreign.
senses.example: Her extravagant wanderings took her across three continents before she turned thirty.

senses.definition: Extreme; wild; excessive; unrestrained.
senses.example: extravagant acts, praise, or abuse

senses.definition: Exorbitant.
senses.example: The hotel charged extravagant prices for a bottle of water in the lobby.

senses.definition: Profuse in expenditure; prodigal; wasteful.
senses.example: an extravagant man

core.definition: Spending or costing much more than is reasonable; excessive, lavish, or over the top.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on STRAV, and the middle syllables are quick schwa sounds. Don't pronounce the middle 'a' as a long 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative (wasteful or excessive), but positive for generous or dramatic gestures; context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for spending, parties, gifts, and claims: 'an extravagant wedding' or 'extravagant promises'. Calling a person extravagant may sound like criticism. Friendlier options are 'lavish', 'generous', or 'over the top'.

distinctions.note: Lavish is more neutral or positive about generous spending; extravagant more often implies excess or waste.
Excessive simply means too much; extravagant adds the idea of costly indulgence or showiness.
Expensive describes price only; extravagant describes spending that goes beyond reason.

examples.everyday: They threw an extravagant birthday party with a live band and fireworks.
examples.professional: The proposal promises extravagant returns, which makes me suspicious of the assumptions behind it.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's extravagant claim that all knowledge is sensory outruns what the evidence can support.

nuance.analogy: Like ordering every appetizer on the menu: impressive, but well beyond what you need.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extravagans, 'wandering outside', from extra 'outside' and vagari 'to wander'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for expensive when it implies excess.
Calling someone's gentle generosity extravagant; it sounds like criticism.

extravagant.etymology: Middle English *extravagaunt*, from Middle French *extravagant* and its etymon Medieval Latin *extravagans*, present participle of *extravagor* (“to wander beyond”), from Latin *extra* (“beyond”) + *vagor* (“to wander, stray”).

senses.definition: To report immediately any condition likely to cause a failure, rather than attempting to continue.
senses.example: Our team decided to fail fast, so the broken API call surfaced during testing instead of production.

senses.definition: To fail earlier rather than later, thus minimizing the fallout and allowing for timely redeployment of resources to another business case or business model.
senses.example: fail fast and pivot

core.definition: To detect a problem early and stop or report it immediately, instead of continuing with a flawed approach, so that losses stay small.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'fast', with 'fail' carrying secondary stress. Link the words smoothly, so it sounds like 'fay-lFAST' with the 'l' moving into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Positive in engineering and business culture, where it is praised as a way to learn quickly; it can sound negative if used to mean carelessness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fail fast' mainly in software development, startups, and product management, often in phrases like 'We should fail fast and iterate'. It is a cultural slogan, so saying it in a meeting signals agile thinking. In a non-tech setting it may sound odd or flippant.

distinctions.note: 'Fail safe' means a system is designed so that a failure leaves it in a safe state, while 'fail fast' means failures are surfaced quickly so they can be fixed.
'Fail forward' emphasizes learning from failure and moving on, while 'fail fast' emphasizes detecting failure early.

examples.everyday: My sister says she wants to fail fast on the new recipe, so she's trying a small batch first.
examples.professional: Let's fail fast on this prototype and test the checkout flow with real users this week.
examples.analytical: The design philosophy of 'fail fast' assumes that early, visible errors are cheaper than hidden ones discovered in production.

nuance.analogy: Fail fast is like a smoke alarm: it goes off early and loudly, so you can respond before the whole house burns down.
nuance.etymology: A modern software and business phrase; its origin is not precisely recorded.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'fail' instead of 'fast' so that it sounds like 'FAIL fast' in an unnatural way.
Using it as a noun phrase, as in 'a fail fast'; it is normally a verb phrase or adjective 'fail-fast'.

senses.definition: An automatic switch to a secondary system on failure of the primary system, such as a means for ensuring high availability of some critical resource (such as a computer system), involving a parallel backup system which is kept running at all times, so that, upon detected failure of the primary system, processing can be automatically shifted over to the backup.
senses.example: When the primary database crashed, the system's failover switched traffic to the standby server within seconds.

core.definition: An automatic switch to a backup system when the main system fails, so that service continues with little or no interruption.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, FAYL. The final syllable is the American 'r-colored' schwa, so say 'ver' with the tongue curled, not 'vur' or 'ov-er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is a positive feature in system design, valued for reliability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'failover' in IT, cloud computing, and database administration, for example 'The database has automatic failover.' As a verb it is often written 'fail over', as in 'The server failed over to the standby.' In non-technical conversation the word is unusual, and people would say 'backup' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Redundancy' is the general design principle of having spare components, while 'failover' is the specific act of switching to one of those spares.
A 'backup' is a copy of data or a spare system, while 'failover' is the automatic switch that moves service onto it.

examples.everyday: My bank's app stayed up during the outage, so I guess they have some kind of failover system.
examples.professional: Our production database has automatic failover, so the standby replica should take over within thirty seconds if the primary goes down.
examples.analytical: A failover design trades some consistency guarantees for availability, which is a tradeoff the architecture must justify explicitly.

nuance.analogy: Failover is like a backup generator that starts within seconds when the power goes out, so the lights never fully go dark.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from 'fail' and 'over', describing a switch over to another system after a failure.
common_mistakes: Writing 'fail over' as one word in a verb context; the verb is two words, 'fail over'.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'oh-ver' with a full vowel instead of an 'r-colored' ending.
patterns: [C, U] failover to sth (= a backup)

senses.definition: To make fertile.
To inseminate.

core.definition: To make something fertile; especially to fertilize an egg or inseminate a female animal. A technical term in biology.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FEK, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa. The final -ate is a long ay sound, so the word rhymes with date, not with fed or feed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; the word sounds clinical and can feel grand or stiff in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use fecundate in everyday speech. Biologists, veterinarians, and agricultural scientists may use it, but most Americans say fertilize, impregnate, or pollinate for plants. Use it in scientific writing or formal description, and avoid it in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Fertilize is the common word for both animals and plants, used in everyday and scientific speech; fecundate is a rarer, more technical synonym.
Inseminate usually refers to introducing sperm or pollen, often in animal breeding; fecundate is broader and can mean making something fertile in general.

examples.professional: The breeding team plans to fecundate the mares in the morning, and we'll log the results by evening.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of how the male seed fecundates the female matter shaped centuries of biological thought.

nuance.analogy: To fecundate is like watering a seed so it can finally grow, turning a potential into a living thing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fecundare, to make fruitful, from fecundus, fruitful.
common_mistakes: Using fecundate for ordinary fertilizing in everyday talk, where Americans would say fertilize
Confusing it with fecund, the adjective meaning fruitful, and using fecund as a verb

fecundate.etymology: From Latin *fecundātus*, perfect passive participle of *fecundō*, see *-ate*.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a league or treaty; derived from an agreement or covenant between parties, especially between nations.
senses.example: The federal treaty bound both kingdoms to defend each other against invasion.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the national government level in a federal nation, as opposed to state, provincial, county, city, or town.
senses.example: Federal agencies like the IRS collect taxes, while the state handles driver's licenses.

senses.definition: Relating to covenantalism.
senses.example: federal theology

senses.definition: A federal agent or (chiefly law-enforcement) official.
senses.example: Two federals in dark suits showed up at the warehouse without warning.

senses.definition: A law-enforcement official of the FBI.
senses.example: The federal who interviewed me at the bank was polite but very thorough.

senses.definition: A supporter of federation.
senses.example: He was a committed federal, arguing that the colonies should unite under one congress.

senses.definition: A Union soldier in the American Civil War.
senses.example: My great-great-grandfather enlisted as a federal in 1862 and fought at Antietam.

core.definition: Relating to the national government of a country, such as the United States, as opposed to state or local government.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FED. The middle syllable is weak and often sounds like ruh, so the word has three syllables, not four. Do not say FEH-day-ral.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a level of government without judgment, though it can sound official or serious.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, federal almost always means the national government in Washington, D.C., in contrast to state, county, and city government. You will hear it in phrases like federal law, federal court, and federal agent. The older religious sense, covenantal, is rare in everyday US speech.

distinctions.note: National can describe anything relating to a whole nation, such as a national holiday; federal specifically refers to the central government in a system where power is shared with the states.
State describes the government of one of the fifty states; federal refers to the national government above them, so the two are often contrasted.

examples.everyday: My cousin works for a federal agency, so she's always complaining about new rules from Washington.
examples.professional: We need to confirm that the dataset meets federal privacy requirements before we share it with partners.
examples.analytical: The argument turns on whether federal authority can override state law in matters of civil rights.

nuance.analogy: Federal is like the head office of a national franchise, setting company-wide rules while each local shop keeps some decisions.
nuance.etymology: From Latin foedus, treaty or covenant, through federalis.
common_mistakes: Using federal to describe any national government; a unitary country such as France is not described as federal
Saying FED-ruh-lee, with an extra syllable and a long e ending instead of -ul

senses.definition: In terms of finance or money.
senses.example: financially responsible

core.definition: With regard to money or finances; in terms of how money affects a person, business or situation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NAN, the second syllable. The first syllable is a reduced uh, and the ending is a light lee sound. Do not add extra syllables such as 'fy-nan-see-uh-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive ('financially secure') or negative ('financially struggling') depending on the adjective it describes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use financially in news, family planning and work conversations: financially secure, financially independent, financially responsible. In casual speech people often say money-wise we're fine. Using financially to mean in the field of finance sounds stiff, so use financial for that meaning.

distinctions.note: Economically refers to the economy or economics in general; financially refers to a person's or organization's money.
Money-wise is informal speech; financially is the more formal and written choice.
Monetarily is rare and usually concerns the value of money or currency, not personal finances.

examples.everyday: We're financially okay, but we're saving more now that the kids are in college.
examples.professional: The vendor is financially stable, so the contract shouldn't carry much payment risk.
examples.analytical: A country may be politically strong yet financially fragile, a gap that historians often overlook.

nuance.analogy: Like checking the fuel gauge: it shows the money side of the trip, separate from how the car is driving.
nuance.etymology: From financial, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing financially before a noun, as in 'financially problems'; use it before an adjective, as in 'financially stable'.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'FI-nan-cial-ly'; the stress belongs on NAN.

senses.definition: The mortal body of a human being, contrasted with the spirit or soul.
senses.example: Many theologians debate how the spirit and the flesh relate in human life.

senses.definition: The evil and corrupting principle working in man.
senses.example: Paul warns that the flesh wars against the spirit in every believer.

senses.definition: The soft tissue of the body, especially muscle and fat.
The skin of a human or animal.
Bare arms, bare legs, bare torso.
senses.example: The tank top left much of his flesh exposed to the cold wind.

senses.definition: Animal tissue regarded as food; meat (but sometimes excluding fish).
senses.example: Our butcher sells only flesh from animals raised on nearby family farms.

senses.definition: The human body as a physical entity.
The soft, often edible, parts of fruits or vegetables.
senses.example: Scoop out the flesh of the ripe avocado and mash it with lime.

senses.definition: A yellowish pink color; the color of some Caucasian human skin.
senses.example: flesh:

senses.definition: To reward (a hound, bird of prey etc.) with flesh of the animal killed, to excite it for further hunting; to train (an animal) to have an appetite for flesh.
senses.example: The huntsman fleshed the young hounds with a reward of raw venison.

senses.definition: To bury (something, especially a weapon) in flesh.
senses.example: The swordsman fleshed his blade deep in the attacker's shoulder.

senses.definition: To inure or habituate someone in or to a given practice.
senses.example: Years of night shifts had fleshed him to the chaos of the emergency room.

senses.definition: To glut.
senses.example: The buffet fleshed the guests until nobody wanted another bite.

senses.definition: To put flesh on; to fatten.
senses.example: The winter feed fleshed the cattle out before they went to market.

senses.definition: To remove the flesh from the skin during the making of leather.
senses.example: The tanner fleshed the hides before soaking them in the lime pits.

core.definition: The soft tissue of a human or animal body, especially muscle and fat, located between the skin and bones.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short E sound, like "fresh". Be sure to keep the "sh" clear at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical or everyday contexts; it can sound blunt or graphic when used about injuries or bodies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flesh in ordinary speech for body tissue, often with words like wound or bone. In religious or philosophical writing it contrasts with spirit and is more formal. Saying "flesh and blood" for family or real people is common and natural.

distinctions.note: Meat means animal flesh eaten as food; flesh refers to body tissue in general, including human.
Body is the whole physical structure; flesh names the soft tissue within it.

examples.everyday: The cut was deep enough that the flesh underneath was showing, so we went straight to urgent care.
examples.professional: The vendor's documentation describes the service as a thin application layer over the flesh of the legacy system.
examples.analytical: Paul often sets flesh against spirit, not as two substances but as two orientations of human life.

nuance.analogy: Like the soft filling inside a sandwich, between the outer bread of skin and the inner frame of bone.
nuance.etymology: From Old English flǣsc, meaning the soft tissue of the body.
common_mistakes: Using flesh as a countable noun in everyday speech without context; it is usually uncountable.
Confusing flesh with meat when talking about food.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is sarx, meaning flesh, the human body, or human nature in its weakness and mortality. Sarx is used both for physical bodies and, in Paul's letters, for the self oriented against God. John 1:14 says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, showing the incarnation as God taking on full human nature. Galatians 5:16-17 contrasts the desires of the flesh with the Spirit, presenting flesh as a force opposed to a life guided by God. Romans 8:5-8 explains that those who live according to the flesh set their minds on what belongs to the flesh, which leads to death.

flesh.etymology: From Middle English *flesch*, *flessh*, from Old English *flǣsċ*, from **flaiski*, from Proto-Germanic **flaiski*, from Proto-Indo-European **pleh₁ḱ-* (“to tear, peel off”).

senses.definition: The quality of being flimsy.

core.definition: The quality of being thin, weak, or poorly made, so that something easily bends, tears, or breaks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLIMZ. The final -ness is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like nus, and the middle vowel is short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes poor quality or unconvincing construction, and it can apply to objects or arguments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to criticize products, furniture, furniture assembly, or reasoning. It is neutral in tone but clearly signals a complaint. It is more often used about things than about people.

distinctions.note: Fragility emphasizes delicacy that can break under stress, while flimsiness emphasizes thinness or weak construction, often seen as a flaw.
Weakness is a broad term for lack of strength, while flimsiness specifically describes something light, thin, or poorly built.

examples.everyday: I could tell from the flimsiness of the patio chair that it would not last the summer.
examples.professional: Testing revealed the flimsiness of the bracket under load, so we need a thicker design.
examples.analytical: The critic exposed the flimsiness of the author's evidence, which rested on a single anecdote.

nuance.analogy: Like a paper bridge that looks like a bridge but sags under the first heavy step.
nuance.etymology: Derived from flimsy, probably from a dialect word for thin or weak.
common_mistakes: Using flimsiness for a person's character, where weakness or spinelessness is more natural.
Misspelling the adjective flimsy with a different vowel.

senses.definition: The reverse, in contrast to the obverse.
senses.example: The coin's flip side showed a wreath, not the president's face.

senses.definition: The converse; opposite, usually negative, inherent aspects or consequences of something.
senses.example: Easy credit has a flip side: people borrow more than they can ever repay.

senses.definition: (dated) The B-side of a phonograph record that carried a less popular recording.
senses.example: My uncle still treasures the flip side of that rare Motown single from 1964.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The less obvious or negative aspect of something; the other side of a situation, often a drawback that comes with an advantage.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SIDE, the second word, while flip gets a lighter secondary stress. Non-native speakers often stress FLIP equally, which makes the phrase sound flat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It introduces a downside after a positive point, so it signals a trade-off rather than a complete failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this constantly in casual talk and in meetings: 'The new apartment is cheaper, but the flip side is the commute.' You can also say 'on the flip side' to start the contrasting point. It sounds natural in nearly any setting, though in formal writing 'drawback' or 'disadvantage' may be more precise.

distinctions.note: A downside is always negative, while the flip side may be neutral or simply the other way of seeing the same fact.
Other side is neutral and literal, such as the other side of a coin or a debate; flip side adds the idea of a contrasting or hidden consequence.

collocations: the flip side of the coin
every benefit has a flip side

examples.everyday: Living downtown is great, but the flip side is that parking is a nightmare.
examples.professional: The new feature speeds up checkout, but the flip side is more load on the database.
examples.analytical: Every gain in efficiency has a flip side, since optimization often trades away robustness.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin: the heads you like come with tails you did not choose.
common_mistakes: Saying 'flip side to' instead of 'flip side of' when introducing the thing it belongs to.
Using it for a neutral alternative; it implies a contrast with something positive.

senses.definition: To vary irregularly; to swing.
senses.example: Gas prices fluctuate daily, so I compare stations before filling my tank.

senses.definition: To undulate.
senses.example: The wheat fields fluctuated gently under the afternoon breeze.

senses.definition: To be irresolute; to waver.
senses.example: I fluctuated between wishing he was back home and wishing I'd never met him.

senses.definition: To cause to vary irregularly.
senses.example: The regulators fluctuated the voltage deliberately to test the circuit's tolerance.

senses.definition: (rare) To rise and fall as a wave; to be tossed up and down the waves.
senses.example: The small boat fluctuated on the swells long after the storm had passed.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Tossed up and down the waves.
senses.example: The fluctuate fishing boats bobbed in the harbor, pitched by the rolling swell.

senses.definition: Wavering, fickle.
senses.example: His fluctuate loyalties made him hard to trust in negotiations.

core.definition: To change up and down irregularly, especially in amount, price, level, or mood.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a quick choo sound, and the final syllable is a clear ayt, not ate; the -tu- sounds like chew.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes change without implying praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fluctuate in business, finance, weather, health, and science contexts, like stock prices or temperatures. In casual speech, people might say go up and down or bounce around. It sounds more precise and professional than go up and down, so it is common in meetings and reports.

distinctions.note: Vary is general and neutral; fluctuate implies repeated changes up and down.
