nuance.analogy: Wherewithal is the fuel in the tank: you may want to drive, but without it the car does not go.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English, from where plus with plus all, literally 'that by which' something is done.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable; the main stress belongs on WAIR.
Using wherewithal for a single tool or item, where 'means' or 'resources' is more natural.

senses.definition: A cereal grain that contains cereal germ, endosperm, and bran, in contrast to refined grains, which retain only the endosperm.

core.definition: A cereal grain that keeps all three of its parts (bran, germ, and endosperm), unlike refined grains, which lose the bran and germ.

pronunciation.tip: The w in whole is silent, so say it like 'hole.' Both words get stress, but the main stress falls on grain, the second word. Keep the r in grain and don't flatten it.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Americans see whole grains as healthy, so the term often appears on food labels and in health advice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase constantly in grocery shopping, nutrition talk, and restaurant menus. Labels often say '100% whole grain,' and the phrase is used in the plural as a category ('eat more whole grains'). It is not a formal term outside food and nutrition, and in casual talk Americans may just say 'whole wheat' for bread made from whole-grain flour.

distinctions.note: Whole wheat is one specific kind of whole grain, made from wheat. Whole grain is the broader category that includes oats, rice, barley, and corn.
Multigrain means a product contains several grains, but those grains may be refined. It does not guarantee that the grains are whole.

examples.everyday: I always check the label to make sure the bread says whole grain.
examples.professional: Our cafeteria menu now uses whole grain pasta and brown rice for every lunch line.
examples.analytical: Nutritional guidelines distinguish whole grains from refined grains because the bran and germ carry most of the fiber and micronutrients.

nuance.analogy: A whole grain is like a complete puzzle, with every piece still in the box, while refined grain is the puzzle after someone has removed the edge pieces.
common_mistakes: Saying 'whole grains' as a single item for one piece of food, when a whole grain is a single kernel of grain.
Pronouncing the w in 'whole,' which is silent.

conversation.text: I switched to whole grain bread.
Whole grain pasta is more filling.
Is this cereal whole grain, or is it mostly sugar?

senses.definition: Withered; lean and wrinkled by shrinkage as from age or illness.
senses.example: The wizened farmer leaned on his cane and smiled at the children playing in the yard.

core.definition: Dried up, shriveled, and wrinkled, especially with age; describing a person who looks small, lean, and old.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'WIZ-und,' not 'WIZ-eh-nd.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes age or illness in a vivid way and can sound sympathetic or a little harsh depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wizened mostly in writing and descriptive speech about people or things, such as an old farmer's face or a wizened apple. In casual talk people usually say 'shriveled' or 'wrinkled' instead. Calling a living person wizened can sound unkind, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Wrinkled describes any surface with folds, while wizened implies the whole body or thing has shrunk and dried out.
Frail describes weakness of body; wizened focuses on a dried, shrunken appearance.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's hands were small and wizened, but she could still shell peas faster than anyone.
examples.professional: The photographer's portfolio included portraits of wizened fishermen, which the client loved for their character.
examples.analytical: The novelist uses the wizened body of the old king to suggest that power itself has decayed along with his health.

nuance.analogy: A wizened apple is like a grape that has been left in the sun and became a raisin: the shape is still there, but the life has dried out of it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'wisen' (to wither), related to Old English 'wisnian' (to wither).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as a full vowel, like 'WIZ-eh-nd.'
Using wizened for a healthy, youthful person as a compliment.

senses.definition: A family or other group of wild wolves.
senses.example: Biologists tracked a wolfpack of nine animals moving through the snowy valley at dawn.

senses.definition: (historical) During World War II, any of various marauding groups of submarines, especially German submarines that patrolled the North Atlantic and preyed upon merchant ships.
senses.example: My grandfather served on a destroyer that hunted for a German wolfpack in the Atlantic.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To gang up on a solitary target, in the manner of a pack of wolves.
senses.example: The three older boys wolfpacked the new kid at recess, cornering him by the fence every day.

core.definition: A group of wolves that hunts together; also a group of people who work together to pursue or pressure a target.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The vowel in pack is the short a of cat, and the word is often written as two words, wolf pack, so don't add a pause if you say it fast.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for wolves; negative for people, suggesting coordinated aggression or unfair pressure on a target.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wolfpack in conversation about animals, sports, and business. The word can be playful, as with the North Carolina State Wolfpack, or critical, as when reporters or analysts gang up on someone. Both wolfpack and wolf pack appear in print, and either spelling is acceptable.

distinctions.note: Pack is general for any group of animals or people; wolfpack emphasizes coordinated hunting or pursuit.
Mob suggests a disorderly crowd driven by emotion, while wolfpack suggests organized, deliberate pursuit.
Gang usually implies criminal activity or youth groups; wolfpack describes a group acting together against a target.

examples.everyday: At the lunch buffet, the kids formed a wolfpack around the pizza and emptied the tray in two minutes.
examples.professional: Three analysts hunted the stock as a wolfpack, all downgrading it within the same hour.
examples.analytical: The essay examines how online crowds can behave like a wolfpack, pursuing a target through coordinated reinforcement rather than individual malice.

nuance.analogy: A wolfpack is like a team that separates one target from the group and wears it down together.
nuance.etymology: From wolf and pack.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing pack with the long a of pay instead of the short a of cat.
Using wolfpack as a verb without the preposition, as in they wolfpacked the reporter without a noun phrase.
Assuming the word always refers to animals, when it is often used for people.

senses.definition: In a wondrous manner.

core.definition: In a way that inspires wonder; marvelously, or to an astonishing degree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ous ending is reduced to 'uhs', not 'ous' as in 'famous', and the final -ly is a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests delight or awe, and it can sound poetic or slightly old-fashioned in ordinary speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wondrously mostly in literary writing, poetry, and some religious or nature writing. In everyday speech, 'wonderfully' is the normal choice, as in 'wonderfully warm' or 'wonderfully simple.' Using wondrously in casual talk can sound deliberately lofty or playful.

distinctions.note: Wonderfully is the everyday word for 'very good' or 'to a great degree'; wondrously is more literary and emphasizes awe.
Marvelously is common and admiring but lighter in tone; wondrously suggests something close to sacred or poetic astonishment.

examples.everyday: The sunset over the lake looked wondrously pink, so we stayed out until it got dark.
examples.professional: The old code ran wondrously fast after we fixed the caching bug, though nobody on the team fully understands why.
examples.analytical: Dickinson writes wondrously about ordinary things, turning a bird or a bee into a window onto eternity.

nuance.analogy: Like a painter who makes a simple landscape glow with light that seems to come from somewhere beyond it.
nuance.etymology: From wondrous (wonder plus the adjective suffix -ous) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing -ous as a full syllable, 'WUN-drus-LEE' with extra stress, instead of the reduced 'uhs'.
Choosing wondrously in everyday speech where wonderfully is more natural.

senses.definition: The excessive, often unnecessary, use of words.

core.definition: The use of more words than necessary; excessive length in speech or writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ness ends in a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'nus', and the middle syllable is a short 'dee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a fault in writing or speech, though it can be neutral when describing a style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wordiness in professional feedback, such as writing reviews or code comments, to say a text could be shorter. Because it sounds like criticism, a softer phrase such as 'Let's tighten this up' is often better. In casual speech, people say 'long-winded' more often.

distinctions.note: Verbosity is the more formal or technical word for the same quality, often used in academic or literary criticism.
Redundancy means repeating information already stated, which is one cause of wordiness rather than the same thing.
Length is simply how long something is, while wordiness means unnecessary words, so a long text can still be concise.

examples.everyday: My uncle's stories are full of wordiness, so I keep asking him to get to the point.
examples.professional: The proposal has too much wordiness; cut it to two pages and the decision makers will actually read it.
examples.analytical: Wordiness is not merely a stylistic flaw; it can conceal weak reasoning behind an impressive amount of text.

nuance.analogy: It is like a sweater with extra yarn: it covers the same body but gets in the way.
nuance.etymology: From wordy, from word, with the suffix -ness, from Old English -nes, meaning a state or quality.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable too strongly; the first syllable carries the main stress.
Using wordiness for a long text that is clear; it means unnecessary words.
Spelling it wordyness; when -y becomes -iness, the y changes to i.

senses.definition: To form letters, words or symbols on a surface in order to communicate.
senses.example: The pupil wrote his name on the paper.

senses.definition: To be the author of (a book, article, poem, etc.).
senses.example: My uncle writes newspaper articles for The Herald.

senses.definition: To compose and send written information (to).
senses.example: Please write to me when you get there.

senses.definition: To compose and send (written information or a written message, e.g. a letter) to.
senses.example: Please write me a letter. Please write a letter to me.

senses.definition: To convey a fact to someone via writing.
senses.example: Jimmy wrote me that he needs more money.

senses.definition: To show (information, etc) in written form.
senses.example: The due day of the homework is written in the syllabus.

senses.definition: To be an author.
senses.example: I write for a living.

senses.definition: To record data mechanically or electronically.
senses.example: The computer writes to the disk faster than it reads from it.

senses.definition: To impress durably; to imprint; to engrave.
senses.example: truth written on the heart

senses.definition: To make known by writing; to record; to prove by one's own written testimony; often used reflexively.
To sell (an option or other derivative).
To paint a religious icon or a pysanka egg.
The act or style of writing.
The operation of storing data, as in memory or onto disk.
senses.example: How many writes per second can this hard disk handle?

core.definition: To form letters or words on paper or a screen to communicate, or to compose and send a written message.

pronunciation.tip: The w is silent and the vowel is a diphthong, like 'rite' or 'right'. The Americans do not pronounce a 'oo' or 'uh' sound at the start; the vowel moves from ah to ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is the basic everyday verb for communicating in writing, and it has no special emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'write' every day for letters, emails, notes, and text documents, and they often say 'I'll write you' or 'write me when you get there.' In casual speech 'text' or 'email' is often used instead, but 'write' remains standard in formal and workplace settings. A natural reply to 'Can you write me a note?' is 'Sure, what should it say?'

distinctions.note: 'Compose' suggests creating a text carefully, often a longer piece of music or writing, and it sounds more formal than 'write'.
'Text' means sending a short message on a phone, while 'write' can refer to any written message, including a letter or report.

examples.everyday: Can you write down your phone number on this card so I can call you when I get back?
examples.professional: Please write a short summary of the release notes before Friday's review so the team knows what changed.
examples.analytical: The philosopher writes that moral reasoning depends on admitting the limits of one's own knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Writing is like drawing a map for someone else: the words are the lines that carry your meaning to a reader who is not in the room.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'writan', meaning to score, draw, or write.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the w, which is silent, and confusing 'write' with 'right' or 'rite' in speech, though they sound the same.
Saying 'write to me' versus 'write me' inconsistently; both are acceptable in American speech, but 'write to someone' is more common in formal writing.

write.etymology: From Middle English *writen*, from Old English *wrītan*, from **wrītan*, from Proto-Germanic **wrītaną* (“to carve, write”), from Proto-Indo-European **wrey-* (“to rip, tear”).

senses.definition: Someone who does wrong, whether morally, ethically, or in contravention of a law.
senses.example: Get and keep wrongdoers out of your thorp (village).

core.definition: A person who does something morally wrong or breaks the law.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on the first syllable and a weaker secondary stress on 'doer,' not equal stress on both. Pronounce 'doer' as 'DOO-er,' with the r at the end, not 'DOH-wer.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always implies that the person did something bad, though it is less harsh than 'criminal' or 'villain.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wrongdoer' mainly in news, legal, moral or formal contexts, such as 'the wrongdoer was arrested.' In casual talk people more often say 'the one who did it' or 'whoever did this.' For specific legal offenses, Americans usually prefer 'offender' or 'perpetrator.'

distinctions.note: A 'criminal' has broken a specific law, while a 'wrongdoer' may have acted immorally or unfairly without breaking any law.
'Offender' is a legal or formal term for someone who committed a specific offense, while 'wrongdoer' is broader and more moral in tone.
'Sinner' is a religious term for someone who has broken God's law, while 'wrongdoer' is a general word for anyone who does wrong.

examples.everyday: Whoever keyed my car is the real wrongdoer, and I want the security camera footage before I talk to anyone.
examples.professional: We need to hold the wrongdoer accountable, not just reassign the junior staff who followed the instructions.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguished the wrongdoer from the one wronged, but modern legal thought often asks whether intention or only harm defines the wrongdoer.

nuance.analogy: A wrongdoer is like a driver who runs a red light: the problem is the choice made at that moment, not the car itself.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'wrong' and 'doer,' from Old English wrang and don, 'to do.'
common_mistakes: Stressing both syllables equally, like 'RAWNG-DOO-er,' instead of the weaker secondary stress on 'doer.'
Using 'wrongdoer' for a simple mistake, when 'the person who made the error' or 'the one at fault' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The color of sunflower petals and lemons; the color obtained by mixing green and red light, or by subtracting blue from white light; the color evoked by light of wavelength around 580 nm; one of the three primary colors in subtractive color systems.
senses.example: yellow:

senses.definition: The middle light in a set of three traffic lights, the lighting of which indicates that drivers should stop short of the intersection if it is safe to do so.
senses.example: The light turned yellow, so I eased off the gas and stopped behind the crosswalk.

senses.definition: One of the color balls used in snooker, with a value of 2 points.
senses.example: He potted the yellow ball and then lined up the black for the frame.

senses.definition: One of two groups of object balls, or a ball from that group, as used in the principally British version of pool that makes use of unnumbered balls (the yellow(s) and red(s)); contrast stripes and solids in the originally American version with numbered balls).
senses.example: Our pub team plays yellows and reds, so we have to pot the yellow before the black.

senses.definition: A yellow dye or pigment.
senses.example: The painter mixed cadmium yellow with a little white to lighten the sky.

senses.definition: A pen, pencil, crayon, etc. made of yellow pigment.
senses.example: She reached for a yellow to color the sun in her daughter's drawing.

senses.definition: Something, or a part of a thing, which is yellow.
senses.example: The yolk is the yellow of the egg, so separate it carefully.

senses.definition: Any of various pierid butterflies of the subfamily Coliadinae, especially the yellow colored species. Compare sulphur.
senses.example: A yellow fluttered past the garden fence, and I watched it land on the clover.

senses.definition: A yellow card.
senses.example: The referee showed him a yellow for the late tackle, and the crowd booed.

senses.definition: Of a yellow hue.
senses.example: He had a yellow laptop in his bag.

senses.definition: Lacking courage.
senses.example: He was too yellow to confront the manager, so he let the mistake pass.

senses.definition: Characterized by sensationalism, lurid content, and doubtful accuracy.
senses.example: The tabloid ran a yellow story about the senator's secret wedding, with no sources.

senses.definition: Of a hue attributed to Far East Asians, especially the Chinese.
senses.example: Early anthropology texts used yellow as a racial label, a usage now rightly rejected.

senses.definition: Far East Asian (relating to Asian people).
senses.example: The 1920s novel used the phrase yellow peril to describe Asian immigrants.

senses.definition: Synonym of high yellow.
senses.example: Her grandmother described herself as high yellow, a term from an earlier era of American speech.

senses.definition: Related to the Free Democratic Party, a political party in Germany.
senses.example: the black–yellow coalition

senses.definition: To become yellow or yellower.
senses.example: The leaves began to yellow early this year because of the drought.

senses.definition: To make (something) yellow or yellower.
senses.example: Years of cigarette smoke had yellowed the ceiling of the old bar.

senses.definition: (historical) To promote (a captain) to flag rank without command of a squadron, ending his career; to make him a yellow admiral.
senses.example: The Admiralty yellowed him, ending his career without a squadron to command.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Used to indicate that the speaker needs a temporary break from current sexual activity.

core.definition: The bright color of lemons, sunflowers and ripe bananas, located between green and orange on the color spectrum.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light, reduced 'uh' sound rather than a full 'low'. Many learners add an extra syllable or drop the second 'l' when they say it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, positive for sunshine, warmth and cheer, but negative when it means cowardice or in the phrase 'yellow journalism'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use yellow constantly for colors, food and traffic lights, and they call the middle traffic light 'the yellow light', which means slow down and prepare to stop. Calling someone 'yellow' to mean cowardly is old-fashioned slang that can insult, so in casual talk say 'scared' or 'chicken' instead. 'Yellow journalism' refers to sensational, inaccurate reporting.

distinctions.note: Golden suggests a warm, shiny or precious quality, as in golden hair or wheat fields, while yellow is the plain color name.
Amber is a deeper, orange-tinted yellow like honey or tree resin, so it describes a more specific shade than yellow.

examples.everyday: The bananas on the counter are turning yellow, so we should eat them this week.
examples.professional: Please change the warning label to yellow, since red is reserved for critical alerts only.
examples.analytical: Newton's prism experiment showed that white light contains yellow as one band of the visible spectrum.

nuance.analogy: Yellow is one of the first colors children learn to name, like a stop sign's red, recognized at a glance.
nuance.etymology: From Old English geolu, related to Latin helvus meaning pale yellow.
common_mistakes: Dropping the second 'l' to say 'yelow', or stressing the second syllable as 'yel-LOH'.
Reading the yellow traffic light as 'speed up'; it means slow down and prepare to stop.

yellow.etymology: From Middle English *yelow*, from Old English *ġeolwe*, oblique form of Old English *ġeolu*, from **gelu*, from Proto-Germanic **gelwaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **ǵʰelh₃wós*, from **ǵʰelh₃-* (“green, yellow”).

senses.definition: In the early part of growth or life; born not long ago.
senses.example: a lamb is a young sheep

senses.definition: At an early stage of existence or development; having recently come into existence.
senses.example: the age of space travel is still young

senses.definition: (Not) advanced in age; (far towards or) at a specified stage of existence or age.
senses.example: How young is your dog?

senses.definition: Junior (of two related people with the same name).
senses.example: Everyone calls him young Tom because his father, Tom Senior, still runs the hardware store.

senses.definition: Early.
senses.example: The night was still young, so we decided to grab dinner before the movie.

senses.definition: Youthful; having the look or qualities of a young person.
senses.example: My grandmother is a very active woman and is quite young for her age.

senses.definition: Of or belonging to the early part of life.
senses.example: The cynical world soon shattered my young dreams.

senses.definition: Offspring, especially the immature offspring of animals.
senses.example: The lion caught a gnu to feed its young.

senses.definition: To become or seem to become younger.
senses.example: Since he started surfing every morning, my uncle seems to young a little each year.

senses.definition: To cause to appear younger.
senses.example: That silver-blue dye and the new haircut seem to young her by a decade.

senses.definition: To exhibit younging.
senses.example: Field evidence from cross-bedding shows the strata young toward the east.

core.definition: Having lived or existed for a short time; not old, especially in relation to a person's age.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short 'uh' of 'sun' or 'sung', not a long 'oo' or 'oh'. Begin with a clear y glide and end with the ng sound, without adding a g after it.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, suggesting energy and possibility, but 'too young' implies a lack of experience and 'young lady' or 'young man' can sound patronizing to adults.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'young' freely about people, animals and things, such as 'a young family' or 'young trees'. Compliments like 'You look young' are welcome, but addressing adults as 'young man' or 'young lady' can sound condescending in workplaces. In casual speech, 'kid' or 'kids' is often used instead for children.

distinctions.note: 'Junior' usually refers to lower rank or to the younger of two people with the same name, while 'young' describes age in general.
'Youthful' describes a look, manner or energy associated with youth, while 'young' describes actual age.
'New' describes things recently made, while 'young' is used mainly for living things or stages of life.

examples.everyday: My daughter is still too young to ride the big roller coaster.
examples.professional: Our team is young, so we need more mentoring before we hand off the production pipeline.
examples.analytical: The thesis assumes that young believers form their convictions more through community than through doctrine.

nuance.analogy: Think of a young tree: it is still growing, and its height and bark show that its story is just beginning.
nuance.etymology: From Old English geong, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz.
common_mistakes: Using 'more young' for comparisons; say 'younger than' instead.
Lengthening the vowel to 'yoong'; the vowel is short, like in 'sung'.

young.etymology: Inherited from Middle English *yong*, *yonge*, from Old English *ġeong*, from **jung*, from Proto-Germanic **jungaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₂yuHn̥ḱós*, from **h₂yuh₁en-* (“young”).

core.definition: Leah's maidservant, given to Jacob as a secondary wife, who became the mother of Gad and Asher, two of the twelve tribes of Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the final vowel a soft 'uh' sound. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Zilpah is a proper name used mostly in Bible study and in discussions of Genesis and the tribes of Israel. Americans would use it in church, theology class or a Bible study group. In ordinary conversation it would sound unusual unless the topic is the Bible.

examples.everyday: My Bible study partner was surprised that Zilpah had two sons who became tribes, Gad and Asher.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Genesis, I explain that Zilpah's sons were counted among the twelve tribes, though her status was that of a servant.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Zilpah in Genesis 30 shows how the rivalry between Rachel and Leah extended to their maidservants, who were given to Jacob as surrogate mothers.

nuance.analogy: Zilpah is like the surrogate in a family story: her children are fully counted in the family, even though her role was that of a servant.
common_mistakes: Confusing Zilpah with Bilhah, the other maidservant who gave Jacob children.
Mixing up which sons she bore.
nuance.biblical_note: Zilpah was a maidservant given by Leah to Jacob as a secondary wife. The key passages are Genesis 30:9-13, which records that Zilpah bore Gad and Asher and that Leah named them; and Genesis 35:26, which lists her sons among the sons of Jacob born in Paddan-aram. Her story shows how the sons of servant women were fully counted among the twelve tribes.

senses.definition: Pimple.

core.definition: A pimple, especially a small red spot on the skin, most often on the face.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i, like 'sit'. Make the z voiced and keep the final t crisp, not 'zeet' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly embarrassing. It is often used with humor, especially among teenagers, and it can sound childish in formal talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say zit in casual conversation, especially among teens and young adults. Adults may say pimple in more polite or neutral settings, and doctors say acne or lesion. Saying zit in a professional meeting would sound too casual.

distinctions.note: Pimple is the neutral term used everywhere, while zit is more casual and often used for an annoying spot.
Acne is the medical condition with many spots, while a zit is a single spot.

examples.everyday: I woke up with a huge zit on my chin, right before the party.
examples.professional: We need to retouch the zit on the model's chin before the catalog goes to print.
examples.analytical: Acne lesions, which people casually call zits, form when oil and dead skin cells clog the hair follicles.

nuance.analogy: A zit is like a small traffic jam in a pore: oil and dead skin get stuck and swell up.
common_mistakes: Using zit in formal writing, where pimple or acne is better.
Saying 'zeet' with a long vowel instead of a short i.

zit.etymology: origin, first attested as 1960s North American English teenagers' slang.
